SHAREHOLDER DERIVATIVE LAWSUIT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE — SHAREHOLDER DERIVATIVE LAWSUIT INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet relates to Acme, Inc., a stock corporation organized under the laws of California, and to Jordan Lee's status as a shareholder of Acme, Inc. It describes California Corporations Code § 800 — the statute setting the procedural conditions a shareholder must satisfy to bring or maintain a lawsuit "in right of" a corporation, meaning a derivative suit brought on the corporation's behalf to redress a wrong to the corporation itself, rather than an ordinary lawsuit brought in the shareholder's own name for a wrong done directly to that shareholder. Transaction or conduct this information sheet may relate to, if applicable: The board's approval of a related-party asset sale below market value.

This information sheet is educational only. It does not itself constitute a complaint, a demand on the board, or any other filing; does not determine whether Jordan Lee meets § 800's ownership, demand, or any other requirement in any specific case; and does not determine whether a court would excuse Jordan Lee from a requirement described below or require a bond under the statute. This document is not this project's Shareholder and Member Inspection Rights document, which covers a separate, non-litigation right to inspect and copy corporate and LLC records — this document instead focuses on the distinct procedural prerequisites for a shareholder lawsuit brought on the corporation's behalf.

WHAT COUNTS AS A "CORPORATION," "BOARD," AND "SHAREHOLDER" UNDER THIS STATUTE
California Corporations Code § 800 governs any action "instituted or maintained in right of" a domestic or foreign corporation by a holder of shares or voting trust certificates — that is, a derivative suit brought to enforce a claim belonging to the corporation itself. For purposes of this statute, the terms it uses are defined more broadly than they might first appear: "corporation" includes an unincorporated association, "board" includes the managing body of an unincorporated association, "shareholder" includes a member of an unincorporated association, and "shares" includes memberships in an unincorporated association. The statute states plainly that such an action may not be instituted or maintained at all unless both of two separate conditions — described in the clauses below — are satisfied.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "As used in this section, “corporation” includes an unincorporated association; “board” includes the managing body of an unincorporated association; “shareholder” includes a member of an unincorporated association; and “shares” includes memberships in an unincorporated association."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 800(a) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, definitions applicable to the shareholder derivative action statute (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=800.)
  "No action may be instituted or maintained in right of any domestic or foreign corporation by any holder of shares or of voting trust certificates of the corporation unless both of the following conditions exist:"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 800(b) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, both statutory conditions required before a derivative action may proceed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=800.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory prerequisites for a derivative suit — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, nor a claim that these are the only requirements a derivative suit is subject to (for example, this document does not address the separate demand-futility case law and pleading standards that inform how courts apply the demand requirement described elsewhere in this document, or federal or other states' analogous derivative-suit statutes). Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 800) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

FIRST CONDITION — PLAINTIFF MUST HAVE HELD SHARES AT THE TIME OF THE TRANSACTION COMPLAINED OF
The first of the two statutory conditions is a contemporaneous-ownership requirement. The plaintiff must allege in the complaint that they were a shareholder — of record or beneficially — or a holder of voting trust certificates, at the time of the transaction (or any part of it) that they complain of, or that their shares or voting trust certificates later devolved on them by operation of law from someone who did hold them at that time (for example, through inheritance). A shareholder who cannot make that allegation is not automatically barred: the statute lets a court, in its discretion, allow the action to proceed anyway on a preliminary motion and hearing, if the shareholder shows, among other things, that there is a strong prima facie case for the underlying claim, that no other similar action has been or is likely to be brought, that the shares were acquired before the wrongdoing was disclosed to the plaintiff or the public, that the defendant would otherwise be able to keep a gain from a willful breach of fiduciary duty, and that granting relief will not unjustly enrich the corporation or another shareholder.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The plaintiff alleges in the complaint that plaintiff was a shareholder, of record or beneficially, or the holder of voting trust certificates at the time of the transaction or any part thereof of which plaintiff complains or that plaintiff’s shares or voting trust certificates thereafter devolved upon plaintiff by operation of law from a holder who was a holder at the time of the transaction or any part thereof complained of"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 800(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, contemporaneous-ownership requirement for a derivative plaintiff (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=800.)
  "provided, that any shareholder who does not meet these requirements may nevertheless be allowed in the discretion of the court to maintain the action on a preliminary showing to and determination by the court, by motion and after a hearing, at which the court shall consider such evidence, by affidavit or testimony, as it deems material, that (i) there is a strong prima facie case in favor of the claim asserted on behalf of the corporation, (ii) no other similar action has been or is likely to be instituted, (iii) the plaintiff acquired the shares before there was disclosure to the public or to the plaintiff of the wrongdoing of which plaintiff complains, (iv) unless the action can be maintained the defendant may retain a gain derived from defendant’s willful breach of a fiduciary duty, and (v) the requested relief will not result in unjust enrichment of the corporation or any shareholder of the corporation"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 800(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, discretionary court exception to the contemporaneous-ownership requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=800.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, real requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and not a claim about whether any particular shareholder's facts would satisfy either the contemporaneous-ownership rule or the discretionary exception to it. The statute lists five specific factors a court "shall consider" in deciding whether to allow the discretionary exception; this document paraphrases all five but does not resolve how a court would weigh them in any particular case. Both citations below are the same subsection of the same statutory section (§ 800(b)(1)) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

SECOND CONDITION — PLEADING EFFORTS TO SECURE BOARD ACTION, OR THE REASONS FOR NOT MAKING THEM
The second statutory condition is a pleading requirement tied to the corporation's board. The plaintiff must allege in the complaint, with particularity, either their efforts to get the board to take the action the plaintiff wants, or the reasons for not making that effort. The plaintiff must also allege that they informed the corporation or the board, in writing, of the ultimate facts of each claim against each defendant, or instead delivered to the corporation or the board a true copy of the complaint the plaintiff proposes to file. The statute itself gives the plaintiff two paths to satisfy this second condition — pursue a pre-suit demand and plead those efforts, or plead particularized reasons for not making a demand — without specifying in its own text what reasons a court will accept as sufficient to excuse a demand.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The plaintiff alleges in the complaint with particularity plaintiff’s efforts to secure from the board such action as plaintiff desires, or the reasons for not making such effort, and alleges further that plaintiff has either informed the corporation or the board in writing of the ultimate facts of each cause of action against each defendant or delivered to the corporation or the board a true copy of the complaint which plaintiff proposes to file."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 800(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, demand-on-the-board pleading requirement or excuse (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=800.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine pleading requirement tied to board demand or its excuse — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and not a claim about what showing would satisfy a "reasons for not making such effort" allegation in any specific case (that determination is fact-specific and, if contested, is for a court applying this statute and the case law interpreting it, which this document does not catalog). This document also does not address the separate, board-controlled procedure by which a corporation can seek dismissal of a derivative suit through an independent committee's determination that the suit is not in the corporation's best interest — that is governed by different authority than the pleading condition described here. The citation below is a single subsection of a single statutory section (§ 800(b)(2)); no additional independent source was found for this.

A MOTION REQUIRING THE PLAINTIFF TO FURNISH A SECURITY BOND
Separately from the two pleading conditions above, § 800 lets the corporation or an individual defendant who is (or was, at the relevant time) an officer or director move the court, within 30 days after being served, for an order requiring the plaintiff to furnish a bond to secure the potential expenses of defending the suit. The court may extend that 30-day window, for good cause, by up to an additional 60 days. The motion must rest on one or both of two specific grounds stated in the statute: that there is no reasonable possibility the claim will benefit the corporation or its shareholders, or that the moving party (if not the corporation itself) did not participate in the transaction being complained of in any capacity. At the hearing on the motion, the court considers evidence relevant to those grounds and to the probable reasonable expenses — including attorneys' fees — the corporation and the moving party are likely to incur defending the action; if the moving party establishes a probability supporting one of the grounds, the court fixes the bond amount, capped at $50,000, covering expenses that may include amounts the corporation could become liable for under a separate indemnification statute (Corp. Code § 317). A ruling granting the motion does not decide the merits of the underlying claim.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "the corporation or the defendant may move the court for an order, upon notice and hearing, requiring the plaintiff to furnish a bond as hereinafter provided. The motion shall be based upon one or both of the following grounds: (1) That there is no reasonable possibility that the prosecution of the cause of action alleged in the complaint against the moving party will benefit the corporation or its shareholders. (2) That the moving party, if other than the corporation, did not participate in the transaction complained of in any capacity."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 800(c) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, motion for an order requiring a security bond and its grounds (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=800.)
  "the court shall fix the amount of the bond, not to exceed fifty thousand dollars ($50,000), to be furnished by the plaintiff for reasonable expenses, including attorneys’ fees, which may be incurred by the moving party and the corporation in connection with the action, including expenses for which the corporation may become liable pursuant to Section 317."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 800(d) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, $50,000 statutory cap on the bond amount (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=800.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine bond-motion mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. It's worth flagging a common imprecise shorthand for this statute: the bond requirement is sometimes summarized as applying to a shareholder who owns only a "small percentage" of the corporation's shares, but the statutory text quoted here does not condition the motion, or exempt any shareholder from it, based on the size of the plaintiff's ownership stake at all — the two grounds for the motion turn on the claim's likely benefit to the corporation and on the moving defendant's non-participation in the underlying transaction, not on how many shares the plaintiff holds. As a practical matter a shareholder with a small stake is more likely to be the one facing such a motion (a large, institutional shareholder's derivative suit is less likely to be characterized as lacking any reasonable possibility of benefiting the corporation), but that is a practical tendency, not a textual ownership threshold in this statute. This document does not address how a court would evaluate "no reasonable possibility" of benefit in any specific case, or the separate indemnification statute (§ 317) the bond-expense provision cross-references. Citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 800(c), (d)) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

WHAT HAPPENS IF THE BOND IS, OR IS NOT, FURNISHED
The statute sets out concrete consequences tied to the bond. If the court determines a bond must be furnished as to one or more defendants, the action is dismissed as to that defendant or those defendants unless the required bond is furnished within whatever reasonable time the court sets. Conversely, if the plaintiff furnishes a bond in the full $50,000 aggregate amount — whether before or after a motion is made, or before or after any order on that motion — the plaintiff has satisfied the statute's bond requirement and any order for a bond already made, any pending motion on the subject is dismissed, and no further or additional bond may be required. Finally, once a bond motion is filed, no defendant needs to file any pleadings, and the prosecution of the action is stayed, until 10 days after the motion has been resolved.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "If the court, upon the motion, makes a determination that a bond shall be furnished by the plaintiff as to any one or more defendants, the action shall be dismissed as to the defendant or defendants, unless the bond required by the court has been furnished within such reasonable time as may be fixed by the court."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 800(d) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, dismissal for failure to furnish a court-ordered bond (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=800.)
  "If the plaintiff shall, either before or after a motion is made pursuant to subdivision (c), or any order or determination pursuant to the motion, furnish a bond in the aggregate amount of fifty thousand dollars ($50,000) to secure the reasonable expenses of the parties entitled to make the motion, the plaintiff has complied with the requirements of this section and with any order for a bond theretofore made, and any such motion then pending shall be dismissed and no further or additional bond shall be required."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 800(e) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, effect of voluntarily furnishing the full $50,000 bond (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=800.)
  "If a motion is filed pursuant to subdivision (c), no pleadings need be filed by the corporation or any other defendant and the prosecution of the action shall be stayed until 10 days after the motion has been disposed of."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 800(f) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, stay of the action while a bond motion is pending (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=800.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual procedural consequences tied to the bond requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. This document does not address what "such reasonable time as may be fixed by the court" means in any specific case, nor whether or how a dismissal under this provision could be appealed or otherwise challenged. Citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 800(d), (e), (f)) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.
